studies.Reference: Intake of α-linolenic acid and other fatty acids in relation to the risk of bladder cancer: results from the New Hampshire case-control study.
studies.Authors: Brinkman MT, Karagas MR, Zens MS, Schned AR, Reulen RC, Zeegers MP
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: The aim of the present study was to investigate the association between the intake of major dietary fats and fatty acids and the risk of bladder cancer.

sample_size.excerpt: Dietary data were collected from 322 cases and 239 controls, and OR and 95 % CI were calculated using unconditional logistic regression.
sample_size.location: Methods; total_n derived from reported group counts 322 + 239 = 561

cases.excerpt: Dietary data were collected from 322 cases and 239 controls, and OR and 95 % CI were calculated using unconditional logistic regression.

effect_size.excerpt: Borderline statistically significant reduced odds were detected for polyunsaturated fat (OR 0·43, 95 % CI 0·19, 0·98; P for trend = 0·07) and linoleic acid (OR 0·43, 95 % CI 0·19, 0·96; P for trend = 0·06). These fats and fatty acids were highly correlated and following adjustment for each other, the only potential inverse association to remain was for ALA.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Borderline statistically significant reduced odds were detected for polyunsaturated fat (OR 0·43, 95 % CI 0·19, 0·98; P for trend = 0·07) and linoleic acid (OR 0·43, 95 % CI 0·19, 0·96; P for trend = 0·06).
